p: Ulises Hilarión Heureaux Leibert, nicknamed Lilís, was born in Puerto Plata on 21 October 1845. His father, José D'Assás Heureaux Fortune, was born in Cap-Haïtien, Haiti, the son of a judge of the civil court there and a member of his household staff; his mother, Josefa Leibert, was born on the island of Saint Thomas. He spoke French and English fluently as well as Spanish. In the rebellion that followed the Spanish annexation of 1861 he became the principal lieutenant of Gregorio Luperón. In 1876 he organised an uprising that seized Puerto Plata and led to the election of Ulises Espaillat.

When Luperón became president in 1879 and stayed in Puerto Plata, he delegated authority in Santo Domingo to Heureaux. Under the priest Fernando Meriño, president from September 1880, Heureaux was interior minister, and Meriño handed the government to him on 1 September 1882. In 1884 Luperón backed General Segundo Imbert as successor; Heureaux promised to respect the result but had ballot boxes stuffed for General Francisco Gregorio Billini. Billini was driven to resign on 16 May 1885. In the 1886 election the fraud committed by Heureaux was so blatant that supporters of his opponent, Casimiro de Moya, rose in the Cibao Valley, and he suppressed the rising brutally.

In 1888 he exiled Luperón, and the next year he forced Congress to abolish the bar on presidential re-election and to end direct elections. He brought members of both rival factions, the Rojos and the Azules, into his government, and kept an extensive network of secret police and informants, assassinating or exiling the politicians he could not co-opt. Cuban planters who arrived after the Ten Years' War received large tracts of the southeastern coastal plain and built the country's first mechanised sugar mills. His government electrified Santo Domingo, bridged the Ozama River and began a railway from Santiago to Puerto Plata.

In 1888 he borrowed three-quarters of a million pounds sterling from the Amsterdam house of Westendorp, which went bankrupt in 1892. The San Domingo Improvement Co. of New York bought out its claims. In 1897, with the country near bankruptcy, he printed five million dollars of unsecured paper money, the papeletas de Lilís, which ruined many merchants and helped to provoke a revolt among the tobacco planters and merchants of the Cibao. He was killed by Ramón Cáceres on 26 July 1899. The national debt then exceeded 35 million dollars, fifteen times the annual budget; the government declared bankruptcy, and the American military intervened.

notes: The article says of his parents: 'His father was Haitian mulatto and his mother was African'; I gave only their birthplaces and the grandfather's office.
The article spells the paper money 'papaletas de Lilís'; I wrote 'papeletas', the usual Spanish word. Revert if the editor wants the article's spelling.
'the American military intervened' follows the article's last sentence, which gives no date; none given.
Presidential terms in the lede (1882-84, 1887-89, from 30 April 1889) are covered by the existing description and not repeated.
